w: Home of Arsenal FC since 2006, built on an industrial and waste-disposal site in Ashburton Grove after the club left Highbury. Seats about 60,700, one of England's largest football grounds, and cost GBP 390 million. Renowned pitch quality has earned it the nickname 'the Carpet' among fans and press.
_facts: Built on former Ashburton Grove industrial site

w: Scotland's national football stadium, in Mount Florida, owned by the Scottish FA. Opened 1903, it was the world's largest stadium until 1950 and hosted the 1960 European Cup final between Real Madrid and Eintracht Frankfurt before a record 127,621 fans, still the highest attendance ever at a European Cup final.
_facts: Home of Scotland national football team

w: Home ground of 1.FC Koln, built on the site of two earlier Mungersdorfer stadiums. Hosted matches at UEFA Euro 1988, the 2006 FIFA World Cup, the 2020 UEFA Europa League final played behind closed doors, and UEFA Euro 2024. Local utility RheinEnergie holds the naming rights.
_facts: Hosted 2006 World Cup and Euro 2024 matches
2020 Europa League final played here behind closed doors

w: Home of Benfica since it opened on 25 October 2003, replacing an earlier stadium of the same name. Seats 68,100, the largest capacity in Portugal, designed by HOK Sport at a cost of EUR 160 million. Hosted the Euro 2004 final and the 2014 and 2020 UEFA Champions League finals.

Built on the site of the demolished Lansdowne Road Stadium and opened 14 May 2010, seating 51,711. Home to the Ireland rugby union team and the Republic of Ireland football team, jointly run by the IRFU and FAI. Hosted the 2011 and 2024 UEFA Europa League finals as Ireland's first UEFA Category 4 stadium.
s: Ireland's rugby and football home since 2010
_facts: Home of Ireland rugby and football teams
Built on former Lansdowne Road site, opened 2010

w: Built 1999-2002 for Turkey's failed bid to host the 2008 Olympics, at a cost of about USD 140 million. Seats 77,563 and holds UEFA's top 5-star rating and IAAF track and field certification. Staged the 2005 Champions League final between Milan and Liverpool, one of the greatest comebacks in the competition's history.
_facts: Built 1999-2002 for a failed Olympic bid
Hosted 2005 Champions League final, Milan vs Liverpool

w: Centrepiece of the 1952 Summer Olympics, hosting athletics, show jumping and the football finals, and Finland's largest stadium, in the Toolo district. Also staged the 1983 and 2005 World Athletics Championships and the 1957 Bandy World Championship. Reopened August 2020 after a four-year renovation.
_facts: Main venue of the 1952 Summer Olympics

w: Built for the 1935 Brussels International Exposition on the Heysel plateau and inaugurated 23 August 1930 before a crowd of 70,000, with Crown Prince Leopold opening it. Renamed for King Baudouin after his 1993 death. Sits beside the Atomium and Mini-Europe park, near the Heysel metro station.
_facts: Opened 23 August 1930 on the Heysel plateau
Named after King Baudouin after his 1993 death

w: Known as the Amex, home of Brighton and Hove Albion since the club took possession on 31 May 2011. Seats 31,876, the second-largest ground in South East England. Hosted 2015 Rugby World Cup and UEFA Women's Euro 2022 matches, plus Brighton's first European tie in 2023 against AEK Athens in the Europa League.
_facts: Home of Brighton and Hove Albion since 2011

w: Also known as Upton Park, this was West Ham United's home from 1904 to 2016, closing capacity 35,016. Charlton Athletic briefly groundshared here in the early 1990s. The final match, 10 May 2016, was a 3-2 win over Manchester United; West Ham then moved to London Stadium and the ground was demolished.
_facts: Home of West Ham United, 1904 to 2016
Last match 10 May 2016 v Manchester United

w: Main stadium of the 1928 Summer Olympics, originally holding 31,600 and later expanded to 64,000 after Rotterdam's De Kuip stadium opened in 1937. Ajax played internationals here until 1996. A later renovation stripped the added tier, cutting capacity to 22,288 and restoring it for track and field.
_facts: Main venue of the 1928 Summer Olympics

w: Home of Ferencvarosi TC, built on the site of the demolished Florian Albert Stadium, known commercially as the Groupama Arena. Holds 22,000, briefly Hungary's largest stadium between the 2017 demolition of the Ferenc Puskas Stadium and the 2019 Puskas Arena opening. Sponsor naming is barred at FIFA/UEFA games.
_facts: Built on the site of the former Florian Albert Stadium

w: Named after Real Madrid legend Alfredo di Stefano (1926-2014), a forward who starred in the club's early European Cup dynasty. The stadium is used by Real Madrid Femenino and Real Madrid Castilla, the club's women's and reserve teams, at the Valdebebas training complex.
s: Named for Real Madrid great di Stefano
_facts: Named after Real Madrid player Alfredo di Stefano
Used by Real Madrid Femenino and Castilla

w: Known as the Gtech Community Stadium, home of Premier League club Brentford since it opened in 2020. Seats 17,250 and is designed for both football and rugby union. Built as the centrepiece of a wider regeneration of the surrounding area, it also hosted matches during UEFA Women's Euro 2022.
_facts: Suitable for football and rugby union

w: Home of Real Club Deportivo Mallorca, built for the 1999 Summer Universiade in the Can Valero industrial zone. Seats 25,736, the largest stadium in the Balearic Islands, and replaced the club's old Lluis Sitjar ground under a 50-year agreement signed in 1999. Its bowl design leaves room for expansion to over 40,000.
s: Real Mallorca's home, biggest in the Balearics
_facts: Home of Real Club Deportivo Mallorca
Capacity 25,736, largest in the Balearic Islands
Club holds a 50-year agreement signed in 1999

w: Headquarters of the Scottish Rugby Union and national stadium of the Scotland rugby team, seating 67,144, the largest ground in Scotland and fifth-largest in the UK. Opened 21 March 1925 with a Scotland win over England that completed a Grand Slam. Has also hosted American football, rugby league and football matches.
_facts: Home of Scotland national rugby union team
Opened 21 March 1925 with a Scotland Grand Slam win
Owned by the Scottish Rugby Union

w: Home ground of RC Strasbourg, commonly called 'la Meinau', owned by the Strasbourg municipality and rented to the club. Hosted a 1938 World Cup match, two Euro 1984 games and the 1988 Cup Winners' Cup final. Pope John Paul II celebrated Mass here in 1988, and the ground has also staged concerts.
s: RC Strasbourg's home, 1988 Cup Winners' Cup final
_facts: Hosted the 1988 Cup Winners' Cup final

w: Sits in Silesian Park in Chorzow and was Poland's national football stadium for decades before Warsaw's National Stadium opened. Closed for reconstruction 2009-2017, reopened with a fully covered capacity of 54,378. Hosts the Kamila Skolimowska Memorial Diamond League meeting and staged 2023 European Games athletics.
_facts: Poland's national football stadium for decades
Hosts the Kamila Skolimowska Memorial Diamond League meeting

w: Home of Blackpool FC since 1901, the club's third ground after Raikes Hall Gardens and the Athletic Grounds. Its three stands are named for club legends Stan Mortensen, Jimmy Armfield and Stanley Matthews. Record attendance of 38,098 came against Wolves on 17 September 1955; it also hosted 2005 Women's Euro matches.
_facts: Stands named for Mortensen, Armfield and Matthews

w: Current home of Dynamo Dresden, named after German middle-distance runner Rudolf Harbig. Sports facilities have stood on the site, the Guntzwiesen, since 1874, and the ground has irregularly hosted German national team fixtures since 1911.
s: Dynamo Dresden's home, sports site since 1874

w: Home of Calcio Catania in the Cibali district, still commonly called the Cibali stadium locally. Built in 1935 by architect Raffaele Leone, it holds 23,266 and was renamed in 2002 for former club chairman Angelo Massimino. Also hosted Jolly Componibili Catania, the women's side that won the 1978 Scudetto.
_facts: Built in 1935 by architect Raffaele Leone
Renamed for chairman Angelo Massimino in 2002

w: Former football stadium in Aixovall, in the parish of Sant Julia de Loria near Andorra la Vella, commercially named DEVK-Arena. Held 1,000 seated spectators. Together with the Estadi Comunal d'Andorra la Vella it staged all matches of Andorra's top two football divisions, the Primera and Segona Divisio.
s: Small ground hosting Andorra's top leagues
_facts: Hosted matches of Andorra's Primera and Segona Divisio
Located in Sant Julia de Loria parish

w: Home of Brentford FC from its opening in September 1904 until August 2020, in a residential part of the London Borough of Hounslow. Famous as the only English league ground with a pub on each of its four corners. Its name refers to the griffin in the logo of Fuller's Brewery, once owner of the orchard it was built on.
s: Brentford's old ground, a pub on each corner
_facts: Only English league ground with a pub on each corner
Named for the griffin in Fuller's Brewery logo

w: Owned by the Irish Rugby Football Union, this Dublin stadium was primarily used for rugby union and football internationals before being demolished in 2007 to make way for the Aviva Stadium, which opened on the same site in 2010. It took its name from the adjacent street in Ballsbridge.
s: Dublin's rugby ground, replaced by the Aviva
_facts: Owned by the Irish Rugby Football Union
Demolished 2007, replaced by the Aviva Stadium in 2010
Named after the adjacent Lansdowne Road

w: Former home of Servette FC, built in 1930 for that year's Coupe des Nations tournament and holding 9,250. Hosted four matches of the 1954 FIFA World Cup, one of the tournament's host venues in Switzerland. Closed in 2002 when Servette moved to the newly built Stade de Geneve.
s: Servette's old ground, 1954 World Cup venue
_facts: Hosted four matches of the 1954 FIFA World Cup
Built in 1930 for the Coupe des Nations

w: Home of HNK Rijeka football club for most years since 1918, wedged between steep cliffs of an old quarry and the Adriatic shore. Croatia's national team has never lost here since first playing at Kantrida in 1990. Seats around 10,600 and is slated for reconstruction with a new stadium planned on the same site.
s: Rijeka's cliffside ground, Croatia's unbeaten venue
_facts: Home of HNK Rijeka since around 1918
Croatia national team unbeaten here since 1990
Site squeezed between sea cliffs and the Adriatic

w: Home of Cordoba CF on a 50-year lease, originally an oval 15,425-seat ground with an athletics track before a 2004 remodelling made it football-only, with rebuilt two-tiered stands. On 25 April 2001 it hosted Spain's national team in a 1-0 win over Japan. Naming rights sold to Bahrain Victorious in 2025.
_facts: Home of Cordoba CF on a 50-year lease
Originally 15,425 seats with an athletics track
Naming rights sold to Bahrain Victorious in 2025

w: Home ground of FC Antibes, named after the neighbouring Fort Carre, and also used by the town's local athletics club. A modest multi-use venue with a capacity of around 4,000, it serves mainly football fixtures in this stretch of the French Riviera.
s: FC Antibes' ground, named for Fort Carre
_facts: Named after the adjacent Fort Carre
Also used by the local athletics club

w: Home of Oldham Athletic since Pine Villa took over the ground in 1899, originally opened in 1896 as the Athletic Ground for Oldham County. Sits at the northwestern edge of Oldham. Oldham RLFC has also played home matches here since leaving Watersheddings in 1997, and it briefly hosted American football in the 1980s.
_facts: Opened in 1896 as the Athletic Ground
Also home to Oldham RLFC rugby league
Briefly hosted American football in the 1980s

w: Former home of Ajax, opened 1934 to replace the club's earlier Het Houten Stadion. Held up to 29,500 at peak but only 19,500 by its 1996 closure. The Netherlands team won all five internationals played here, 1973-1992. Ajax then moved to the new Amsterdam Arena, now Johan Cruyff Arena, and De Meer was demolished.
s: Ajax's old ground, demolished for housing
_facts: Netherlands won all five internationals played here
Ajax moved to Amsterdam Arena in 1996

w: Home of Levski Sofia since it opened in 1963, in the Suhata reka neighbourhood, and nicknamed Gerena, meaning 'the flood plain'. Named after Bulgarian footballer Georgi Asparuhov (1943-1971), a Levski legend who died young in a car crash.

Known as the Crown Oil Arena, this multi-purpose ground in the Spotland district of Rochdale is shared by Rochdale AFC and the Rochdale Hornets rugby league club. Seats 10,249, serving both codes for the Greater Manchester town.
s: Shared home of Rochdale AFC and Hornets RL
_facts: Home of Rochdale AFC and Rochdale Hornets RLFC
Located in the Spotland district of Rochdale

w: Built in 1956 in an old stone quarry behind the Jeronimos Monastery in Belem, home to second-division club Os Belenenses. Seats 19,856. The inaugural match was a 2-1 win over Sporting CP, and Pope John Paul II celebrated a Mass here attended by more than 100,000 people. Also used for concerts.
_facts: Home of Clube de Futebol Os Belenenses
Built in 1956 in a former stone quarry
Pope John Paul II held Mass here for over 100,000

w: Home of OFK Beograd, meaning 'Youth Stadium' in Serbian, built by the firm Sportprojekt under architect Karlo Kacl. Nominal capacity of 19,100 but only 10,600 actual seats, and by 2012 it could hold only around a third of its intended crowd due to deteriorating condition.
_facts: Built by firm Sportprojekt, architect Karlo Kacl

w: Multi-purpose indoor arena in Sofia opened in July 2011, seating 12,373 for sport and up to 17,906 for concerts. Designed to host around 30 sports including basketball, volleyball, handball, boxing and gymnastics. Sponsorship has passed from Armeets insurance to the 8888.bg gambling platform since September 2024.
_facts: Seats 12,373 for sport, up to 17,906 for concerts

w: Former multi-use stadium on Hisingen, an island within Gothenburg, opened on 18 August 1935. Served as the home ground of BK Hacken, hosting the club's football matches at a modest capacity of 7,000 spectators before the venue was eventually retired.

Indoor arena in Casalecchio di Reno, metropolitan Bologna, opened December 1993 and previously known as PalaMalaguti. Seats 11,000 for basketball, up to 20,000 for concerts. Home of the Virtus Bologna basketball team, 1996-2017, and served by its own Casalecchio Palasport rail station.
_facts: Served by Casalecchio Palasport railway station

w: Multi-purpose stadium in Wroclaw, home to speedway team Sparta Wroclaw and American football side Panthers Wroclaw. Now holding around 11,000, it was originally slated to be a Euro 2012 venue before the newly built Stadion Miejski was used instead.
_facts: Home of speedway team Sparta Wroclaw
Home of American football team Panthers Wroclaw
Originally proposed as a Euro 2012 venue
